props.title: Malignant

sections.content: James Wan's **Malignant** (2021) marks a wild return to original horror, channeling the giallo-soaked insanity of Basket Case (1982) and Phenomena (1985). The film deliberately subverts modern horror conventions established by Wan's own **The Conjuring** (2013), instead embracing the operatic excess of Italian horror masters like Dario Argento. The neon-drenched visuals and over-the-top practical effects recall the best of 80s body horror while pushing into fresh territory.

sections.content: The film's bold third act reveal transforms it from atmospheric supernatural horror into something far more visceral and unique. This dramatic shift mirrors other genre-bending horror films like **From Dusk Till Dawn** (1996) and **Audition** (1999), where audience expectations are deliberately upended. The practical effects work, particularly in the police station sequence, channels the kinetic energy of **The Thing** (1982) while adding distinctly modern flourishes.

Wan's direction demonstrates clear inspiration from the Italian horror movement of the 1970s and 80s. The saturated lighting schemes and elaborate camera movements echo **Suspiria** (1977) and **Tenebrae** (1982), while the medical horror elements draw from **Re-Animator** (1985). The film's score by Joseph Bishara amplifies these influences with its synth-heavy Goblin-inspired compositions. SUBHEAD: Modern Body Horror Evolution

sections.content: **Malignant** (2021) represents a fresh evolution in body horror, building on foundations laid by films like **Society** (1989) and **Tetsuo: The Iron Man** (1989). The film's creature design and movement choreography create something genuinely new in the genre, while the backstory involving medical experimentation connects to contemporary fears about genetic manipulation seen in films like **Splice** (2009).
